item.title: New Oranje coach Xavi calls Netherlands “university of football”
item.description:
New Oranje coach Xavi calls Netherlands “university of football”

August 25, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

New national head coach Xavi Hernandez said he regarded the Netherlands as the “university of football” as he gave his first press conference in Zeist.

The 46-year-old said it was an “honour” to be appointed by the KNVB as the first foreign coach since Austria’s Ernst Happel led the men’s team to the 1978 World Cup final.

Xavi was the KNVB’s third choice for the job after Pep Guardiola, the former Manchester City coach, opted to take a sabbatical from football and Arne Slot, the former Feyenoord and Liverpool coach, preferred to stay in club football.

He has been given a four-year contract until the end of the next World Cup in 2030, with no conditions tied to the Netherlands’ performance at the European Championships in two years’ time.

Most of Xavi’s playing career was spent at Barcelona, where he won eight La Liga titles, many of them under the tutelage of Guardiola, whose playing style was influenced by Dutch legend Johan Cruyff.

He made his international debut for Spain in a friendly game against the Netherlands in 2000 and 10 years later was one of the pivotal members of the team that won the World Cup in 2010, defeating Oranje in the final.

“My feeling today is that I’m going to the university of football,” Xavi said. “I learned a lot during my career as a player and a coach that I want to give back.

Big family

“I believe a lot in this generation,” he added. “We have a lot of talents, but the important thing for me is to create a team, a group and a big family in order to play well.”

Asked how he felt about being the KNVB’s third choice, ahead of youth team coach Michael Reiziger, Xavi said: “It’s not a bad position after Guardiola and Slot. At least we’re on the podium.”

He added that the Dutch “total football” school was the basis for his own style of football as both a player and a coach.

“To dominate, the game, to take the initiative with the ball, and at the same time our goal is to show to everybody a team with passion, with desire and ambition. That is my philosophy,” he said.

“We are here to compete, we are here to enjoy and we are here to win.”

Senior players

The KNVB’s technical director, Nigel de Jong, said Xavi was identified as a candidate because his footballing philosophy aligned closely with the Dutch team’s ambitions to play “attractive, dominant” football.

The coach said he had not made any decisions about which players he will select, but he had already spoken to current team captain Virgil van Dijk and Barcelona midfielder Frenkie de Jong.

Dutch media have speculated that Van Dijk, 35, and leading scorer Memphis Depay, 32, could be dropped from the squad as part of a clear-out of senior players.

De Jong, who worked with Xavi during the Spaniard’s spell as Barcelona coach from 2021 to 2024, has been struggling with injuries for more than a year and was not fully fit during this year’s World Cup.

The coach also said he had been monitoring AZ Alkmaar’s promising 20-year-old midfielder Kees Smit, who narrowly missed out on the World Cup squad this summer.

Oranje will play their first match under his leadership on September 24, when they take on Germany in the Nations League in Amsterdam. “We haven’t yet decided the [squad] list,” Xavi said. “You will see it in three weeks.”

item.title: Vondelkerk fire investigation ends in mystery, police say
item.description:
Vondelkerk fire investigation ends in mystery, police say

August 25, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

How the Vondelkerk in Amsterdam went up in flames on New Year’s Eve is still unknown, police have said, after months of trying and failing to establish a criminal cause for the blaze.

Investigators had looked into whether the fire was started deliberately and whether fireworks were to blame. Local residents were interviewed, video footage examined and tips about possible arson followed up, but none of it produced any evidence, police said.

It could also not be established whether fireworks caused the fire. Much of the forensic evidence was destroyed in the blaze itself, police said, and no traces of fireworks were found. With no leads left to pursue, the investigation has stalled.

Years to rebuild 
The monumental church on Vondelstraat, close to the Vondelpark, was largely destroyed in the early hours of January 1, when its tower collapsed and much of the roof was lost. It was designed by Pierre Cuypers, the 19th-century architect behind Amsterdam’s Centraal station and the Rijksmuseum, and completed in 1880.

The building served as a Catholic church until it closed in 1977 and has since been used for concerts, offices and community events, with church services returning in 2017. It has been owned since 1996 by heritage restoration body Stadsherstel Amsterdam.

Several fundraising drives were launched after the fire. Stadsherstel said more than €180,000 had been raised within a week, and other appeals brought in tens of thousands of euros more. Rebuilding the church is expected to take years.

item.title: Dutch foundation plans to build underground hospital in Ukraine
item.description:
Dutch foundation plans to build underground hospital in Ukraine

August 25, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A Dutch organisation is trying to raise funds to build a reinforced underground hospital in Ukraine so soldiers can be treated nearer the front line.

Protect Ukraine and a Norwegian foundation, HMM Healthcare, say they have already secured €750,000 in donations for the project, which is expected to cost €2.5 million in total.

The 600 m2 hospital will be built 8 m below ground and made entirely of concrete, allowing wounded service personnel to be treated in what is effectively a giant bunker.

The organisers hope to have the building fully equipped and operational by February 2027.

Jaap Scholten, a Dutch writer and co-founder of Protect Ukraine, said: “The fact that we have raised three-quarters of a million euros in such a short time shows that people in the Netherlands have not forgotten Ukraine.

“But we are not there yet. Every donation brings us closer to a hospital and stabilisation point that can save many lives.”

Protect Ukraine has around 100 volunteers who run regular trips to Ukraine to deliver goods such as medicines, pop-up tents and pick-up trucks.

Scholten, who lives in Hungary, told NOS he started the organisation after watching people in his neighbourhood handing out fresh fruit, energy bars and blankets to Ukrainian refugees.

“Arranging supplies for Ukrainians is the most effective thing you can do to help,” he said. “That’s why I started Protect Ukraine.”

item.title: Many Dutch children hide upsetting online posts from parents
item.description:
Many Dutch children hide upsetting online posts from parents

August 25, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Half of children in the Netherlands aged 10 to 15 sometimes see posts online that frighten or upset them, but many do not tell their parents out of shame or fear of an angry reaction, a government survey has found.

The finding comes as junior digital economy minister Willemijn Aerdts launches a new phase of the government’s Blijf in Beeld (“Stay in the picture”) campaign, which encourages parents to talk to their children about what they encounter online and to agree rules on phone use together.

The survey, commissioned by the economic affairs and climate ministry (EZK), found children in the Netherlands now get their first smartphone at the age of 10 on average. Children most often named Snapchat and TikTok as the places they were most likely to come across something unpleasant.

Talk early
Aerdts said parents should start those conversations while children are young, before the influence of friends grows. “Be curious about what they see, including the nice and funny things,” she said, arguing this makes it easier for children to also raise the frightening or harmful side of social media.

Parents should not judge children for what they do online, she added, and should be open about their own use.

The campaign, developed in part with children’s helpline the Kindertelefoon, comes with a printed card that parents and children fill in together. The ministry said 89.4% of children understood why rules on phone use mattered, and half said they welcomed them.

Waiting for Brussels
Aerdts said platforms were not doing enough to protect children. “The online world is really not yet a safe place for children,” she said, adding that this was why the government wants a minimum age for social media use agreed at European level rather than in national law.

That marks a contrast with France, Spain and Greece, which have moved to set their own age limits. France passed a law last month barring under-15s from social media, though its Constitutional Council then ruled the measure unconstitutional in its current form and the government is redrafting it.

Aerdts has previously said she wants to avoid “a mishmash of rules and regulations that will The European Commission is working on its own proposals: last month researchers advised it to ban social media for children under 13, and commission president Ursula von der Leyen has said she will bring forward a proposal to limit children’s use after the summer.

item.title: Shrinkflation eases but manufacturers turn sneaky, watchdog says
item.description:
Shrinkflation eases but manufacturers turn sneaky, watchdog says

August 25, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Shrinkflation is happening less often than a few years ago, but manufacturers are getting better at hiding it, consumer body the Consumentenbond has found in its latest sweep of Dutch supermarket shelves.

The organisation again found dozens of products whose contents had shrunk without a matching drop in price, and received fewer reports from shoppers than in previous years. But a hard core of producers are now shrinking packs so quietly that customers don’t notice.

The clearest example is Blue Band Vloeibaar, the liquid baking product, which dropped from 750 to 700 millilitres in March 2026 while the bottle and front label stayed exactly the same.

The new volume appears only in small print on the side, and the pack is still described as a “voordeelfles”, or value bottle. The recommended price held at €3.65, so shoppers pay more per millilitre either way.

Shrunk more than once
Some products have now been reduced two or three times over. Andrélon conditioner went from 300 to 250 and then to 200ml; on the last step the price rose from €5.49 to €6.49, a 48% increase per 100ml.

A bag of M&M’s, which held 440 grams in 2020, now contains 363 grams, leaving consumers paying about 10% more per 100 grams.

Manufacturers mostly blamed higher costs for packaging, raw materials, energy and transport. Mars, which makes M&M’s, pointed to recently changed rules it said might bar producers from sharing recommended prices – but, the watchdog said, as far as it could tell no such change had taken place.

Consumentenbond director Sandra Molenaar called on politicians to act. “When there is more in a pack, manufacturers shout it from the rooftops,” she said, “but when the contents shrink, they only adjust it quietly on the back.”

She wants producers required to state a reduction clearly on the pack, or supermarkets made to flag it at the shelf, as is already the law in France.

item.title: Fraudsters using iDeal switch to Wero to snare bank customers
item.description:
Fraudsters using iDeal switch to Wero to snare bank customers

August 25, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Fraudsters are sending out phishing mails to Dutch bank customers to try to take advantage of the switch from the iDeal payment system to Wero.

The fake messages typically tell customers they are due a refund as a result of the transition to Wero, the European-based system set up under efforts to make EU businesses less dependent on foreign digital services.

Victims are told to verify their identity by clicking on a link in the e-mail, which takes them to a page where the criminals can steal their login details.

The online fraud hotline Fraudehelpdesk.nl said it was currently receiving 100 queries a day about suspicious messages regarding iDeal, after a surge in activity in the last few months.

A frequently seen mail in recent days says the handover took place on August 24 and puts customers under pressure to claim their refund before the “deadline”.

Danial van Delft, CEO of Currence, the company that operates iDeal and Wero, told the Telegraaf: “This is a big change in the payments ecosystem and gives people with bad intentions space to abuse it.

“We see fraudsters becoming more and more inventive. They are trying to latch on to every hook and news item.”

iDeal said people should ignore suspicious emails and not click on links. “iDeal will never ask you to confirm personal details by email, start a verification process or install software,” the company said.

item.title: Villagers at centre of asylum row urge council to heal divide
item.description:
Villagers at centre of asylum row urge council to heal divide

August 25, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Residents of a Noord-Brabant village at the centre of a bitter row about plans to accommodate 50 asylum seekers have accused the local council of making the problem worse through its poor communications strategy.

Violent protests were staged in Engelen, on the edge of ’s-Hertogenbosch, after the council announced in April it would be housing a group of teenage boys and girls, all under 18, in a former police station on Beverspijken.

Opponents have staged marches to express their concern about women’s safety, while supporters say they have been subjected to a hate campaign, with swastikas and obscene words spray-painted on their homes.

At a council meeting on Monday night, residents on both sides of the divide appealed to the local mayor, Jack Mikkers, to talk to villagers before the final decision is made next month.

Around 100 people packed into the council chamber in Den Bosch and a side room set up as an overspill location for those who were unable to get into the public gallery.

The council says it has an obligation to accommodate asylum seekers under the so-called “spreading law”, which requires all local authorities to take in a fair share in order to ease overcrowding at the reception centre in Ter Apel, Groningen.

“Spend an evening walking through Engelen, ring people’s doorbells and listen,” said Tamara Govers, who organised one of the marches in May. “Come as a person, not an official, without cameras or press releases.”

Blacklist

Astrid van den Broek, who spoke in support of the plan, called for councillors to stop the threats and intimidation. “My name’s been put on a blacklist,” she said, adding that a man who threatened her when she filmed a group putting up protest signs was at the meeting.

“I’ve told security,” she said. “Don’t talk to me about being concerned about our women’s safety if the shelter goes ahead.”

Other villagers said the municipality had been too slow to respond to the menacing atmosphere in the village. “The shelter has driven a wedge between friendships,” said resident Eva Buijs.

Jack Burg, chair of local campaign group Veilig Engelen, said “better communication” from the council could have prevented the situation escalating.

Burg said the plans did not do enough to address concerns about the impact of the refugee centre on quality of life in the village.

“Conditions and rules have not been worked out,” he said. “We need more than this plan for a suitable accommodation facility. We want clarity, but that’s not what this is.”

Strict conditions

The council has set strict conditions for the centre, including a 10pm curfew and night-time security. Residents will have to move out as soon as they turn 18, most likely to smaller groups in Den Bosch.

The municipality also wants the refugee accommodation agency COA to send equal numbers of girls and boys, but that may be difficult to arrange because five out of six underage asylum seekers are male.

Some residents said they were not against accommodating refugees in the village, but called the empty police station on Beverspijken the “wrong location”.

One group produced data from decibel readings taken from the site that showed levels of 83 decibels had been recorded at night – 18db higher than the level permitted by the local environmental plan.

Others questioned whether the council and the COA could be relied on to stick to their agreeement to make the accommodation centre a temporary facility, pointing out that permits for other locations have been extended at the request of the agency.

item.title: Deadlock looms in budget talks as opposition drive hard bargain
item.description:
Deadlock looms in budget talks as opposition drive hard bargain

August 25, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Talks to secure support from opposition parties for next year’s budget are entering their final days with no sign of a breakthrough.

Jesse Klaver, leader of the left-wing opposition group Pro (previously GroenLinks/PvdA) said the two sides had “not moved a step closer to each other” after emerging from negotiations on Monday.

Michiel Hoogeveen, of the right-wing JA21, accused the coalition parties of “kicking the can down the road”, while the hardline Protestant party SGP said a deal was “a long way off”.

Finance minister Eelco Heinen has a deadline of August 28 to submit a draft budget to the Council of State before the formal presentation of his plans at the state opening of parliament on September 15.

MPs will not vote on the measures until late in the autumn, but the cabinet wants to do a deal with the opposition to secure majority support in both houses before budget day.

Yo-yo politics

Prime minister Rob Jetten said earlier: “This cabinet has big ambitions to make major investments in the next few years in more affordable houses, more security and the economy of the future. It’s good to do that with others if we want to avoid yo-yo politics.”

The minority coalition of D66, VVD and CDA needs the support of 10 opposition MPs in the lower house and 16 senators to pass its legislation.

Asylum minister and deputy prime minister Bart van den Brink, of the CDA, said the government was prepared to take “big steps” to accommodate the opposition groups. But Klaver said he had seen little sign of movement from the coalition.

Pro wants the cabinet to shelve plans to cut welfare spending by €6.5 billion in order to raise money for other departments, chiefly defence, where the Netherlands is striving to hit the new Nato target of 3.5% of GDP.

Wealth taxes

The party argues that the money should be raised by raising wealth taxes instead. “The cabinet seems to be mainly concerned with the position of millionaires in the Netherlands while we are worried about the people who are paying the bills,” Klaver said.

But Heinen’s party, the right-wing liberal VVD, is opposed to wealth taxes and would prefer to make concessions to parties on the right such as JA21 and SGP, who want to see tax cuts instead. But SGP MP André Flach said on Tuesday that the coalition’s plans “are not enough at the moment”.

The SGP, which draws its vote from Bible-Belt communities, wants the cabinet to suspend plans to legalise surrogate motherhood and permit late-term abortions of up to 22 weeks in some hospitals.

The party has teamed up with JA21 to form a right-wing block of 12 seats, which would be enough to give the coalition a majority in the Lower House. However, they would still be short in the Senate, where any right-wing majority depends on the support of the farmers’ party BBB.

BBB key

The BBB has not been invited to the talks so far because of its staunch opposition to the cabinet’s plans to reduce nitrogen pollution, which would require some livestock farmers to give up or drastically reduce the size of their herds.

Party leader Henk Vermeer is meeting Heinen on Tuesday, but the BBB is not expected to compromise on its stance. “Anyone who can count can see they can’t do without us”.

The 20 seats held by Pro would give the cabinet a clear majority in the lower house, while only one small party such as Volt would be needed to pass the budget in the Senate.

But the right-wing VVD is reluctant to rely solely on Klaver’s party, which was kept out of the coalition in February on the insistence of VVD leader Dilan Yesilgöz.

item.title: Dutch cocaine-broker case in Colombia grows to 55 suspects
item.description:
Dutch cocaine-broker case in Colombia grows to 55 suspects

August 25, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

An investigation into two Dutch men accused of brokering cocaine shipments from Colombia has grown into a much wider case, with prosecutors now pursuing 55 suspects, 35 of them already arrested, for drug trafficking, money laundering, extortion, violence and planned kidnappings.

Pre-trial hearings began on Monday at Zwolle district court, broadcaster NOS reported. The two main suspects, Dutch men aged 42 and 47, were arrested in Colombia in February and are still awaiting extradition, which can take more than a year.

The case grew out of a national police investigation opened in January 2025. Prosecutors say the pair connected Colombian cartels with cocaine buyers in the Netherlands and arranged shipments of hundreds of kilos at a time.

Intercepted chat messages then led investigators to a web of associates, and twelve further investigations are now running.

One concerns four men who allegedly prepared to kidnap the girlfriend of a man suspected of stealing a cocaine shipment in 2024, a theft that left a debt of more than €700,000. The kidnapping did not go ahead, and prosecutors say they do not know why.

Another involves two men accused of extorting around 1,000 clients of the sex-work website Kinky, who allegedly faced threats of serious violence unless they paid. Police believe the pair took more than €100,000.

The Netherlands has invested heavily in police cooperation with Colombia, which prosecutors say is now producing results, with several Dutch nationals arrested there. The main suspects’ cases will not be heard in full until they are extradited

item.title: Health inspectors ban webshop from selling weight loss drugs
item.description:
Health inspectors ban webshop from selling weight loss drugs

August 25, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Health inspectors have banned a website from selling unlicensed weight loss drugs that it advertised on social media.

De Peptidekoning sold two medicines prescribed to treat diabetes, semaglutide and tirzepatide, and a third, retatrutide, which is an experimental drug that has not been licensed in any country.

The Health and Youth Care Inspectorate (IGJ) ordered the owners of the website to stop selling all three substances and warned patients not to risk their health with experimental treatments.

It said De Peptidekoning, which trades through several websites including puritybase.com, did not have a license to sell the medicines. “They have not adequately ensured that the medicines meet standards for quality, safety and effectiveness,” the IGJ said.

“The way in which the medicines were offered for sale does not give enough reassurances, which creates risks for public health.”

RTL Nieuws reported that unauthorised traders were profiting from a black market in slimming treatments for people who were not prescribed medicines such as Ozempic, which are only available in the Netherlands to treat diabetes.

Marloes Dankers, of the Utrecht-based Dutch Institute for the Rational Use of Medicine, an advisory body set up by doctors and pharmacists, said: “People are making guinea-pigs of themselves.

“These medicines are still being researched and we don’t know what exactly the risks are. That’s the reason for doing the research.”

Eli Lilly, the American manufacturer developing retratrutide, also urged people not to buy the drug online.

“What is being sold on the black market is not a medicine, it has not been approved or verified in any way and it is not worth the risk,” the company said.
